disclaimer: Every figure in this piece was read in the IBGE primary table (SIDRA) or in the report that produced it, credited to whoever did the work. Nothing here is our own calculation: where there is a division, it is written beside it, and where the number belongs to someone else, their name comes with it.
headline.label: is the official unemployment rate for 2025 — the lowest since the series began in 2012
whatItMisses[0].label: is the composite underutilisation rate: the 6.2 million unemployed PLUS 5.9 million who wanted work and did not look or were not available, PLUS 4.6 million working fewer hours than they need. Almost three times the headline.
whatItMisses[1].label: Brazilians between 25 and 59 — neither too young nor too old — neither work nor look for work. By definition, none of them enters the unemployment rate. That is almost four times the 6.2 million the rate does count.
whatItMisses[2].label: of employed people are in informal work. Odd jobs, app driving, street vending: all of it counts as employment inside the 5.6%.
duel.question: How can there be 5.6% unemployment in a country where more people are on Bolsa Família than hold a formal job?
duel.left.label: people covered by Bolsa Família
duel.left.note: 18.91 million families, average benefit of R$ 683.42 — October 2025
duel.right.label: people in formal employment
duel.right.note: General Register of Employed and Unemployed Workers — February 2026
duel.note: Both sides are people, not families: the report compares beneficiary families with employed individuals, and here the sum was redone in the same unit — 49.4 million people covered against 48.8 million with a formal job.
states.title: Nine states have more families on Bolsa Família than formal jobs
states.extra: Maranhão has 1.66 beneficiaries for every formal job. Across the country there are 38.6 beneficiaries for every 100 formal jobs, and 2,639 municipalities have more Bolsa Família than formal employment. At the opposite end, Santa Catarina has 13 jobs for every beneficiary family, and São Paulo has 12.5 million more formal jobs than beneficiaries.
disincentive.title: The disincentive is not an opinion: it is in the regulation
disincentive.body: A family leaves Bolsa Família when income passes R$ 218 per person. A family of four in which someone lands a formal job on the minimum wage (R$ 1,621) reaches R$ 405 per person — and loses the whole benefit. The government created the Protection Rule: those who cross the threshold keep HALF the benefit for up to 24 months, as long as income stays below half a minimum wage per person. The rule exists because the design of the programme made anyone who found formal work lose the whole benefit.
bpc.label: assistance benefits (LOAS) were being paid in April 2026: 2,675,506 to elderly people and 3,681,079 to people with disabilities. Each is worth exactly one minimum wage — R$ 1,621 in 2026 — because the Constitution sets that floor in article 203, item V.
ghani.title: The sum an economist made with the same data
ghani.body: Alan Ghani, a finance PhD from FEA-USP, published in Gazeta do Povo that, adding the unemployed by the IBGE criterion to those who do not look for work, Brazil would have 72.7 million working-age people not working — a rate of 41%. The calculation is his, not ours, and the starting figure is correct: 66.2 million are outside the labour force.
ghani.caveat: The age breakdown is above: 40% of those 66.2 million are 60 or older, and another 15% are between 14 and 17. That is why this site publishes the 25-to-59 slice — 22.9 million who neither work nor look for work — and not the 41% rate.
question: A country can have, at the same time, the lowest unemployment in its series and more people on Bolsa Família than in formal jobs. Both figures are official and they do not contradict each other — what differs is what they measure. Which of the two did you see in the headline?
participation.title: The rate falls because the base shrinks
participation.body: The unemployment rate divides the unemployed by the labour force — those working or looking. Anyone who leaves that base pulls the rate down without a single job being created. And the base shrank: labour force participation stands at 62.7%, exactly the 2012 level and 1.1 points below the 2019 peak.
cost.title: What the two programmes cost per year
cost.body: Bolsa Família and BPC together come to R$ 270.6 billion in the 2025 federal budget. That is tax money, and it is the bill the "lowest unemployment on record" headline never mentions.
bpc.growth.text: The number of beneficiaries grew 33% in 31 months, from mid-2022 to March 2025, according to a survey reported by CNN Brasil.
